Two focused practice sessions should close that gap before December 12.

covered.title: A matrix is a linear map written in a basis
covered.summary: Everything rests on one unconditional truth: a linear map is determined by what it does to a basis. The matrix just records those images as columns.
points: Matrix multiplication is composition of maps, which is why it is not commutative.

covered.title: Rank–nullity as conservation of dimension
covered.summary: Every input dimension either survives into the image or is crushed into the kernel:
points: Used it to decide injectivity from dimensions alone.

covered.title: Eigenvectors are directions a map only stretches
covered.summary: Solving $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$ is just asking when $A - \lambda I$ crushes some direction, which links straight back to the kernel.

weaknesses.title: Direction of the change-of-basis matrix
weaknesses.misconception: You treated $P$ as converting standard coordinates into $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates, at 90% confidence.
weaknesses.correction: The columns of $P$ are the $\mathcal{B}$ basis vectors written in standard coordinates, so $P$ converts **from** $\mathcal{B}$ **to** standard: $[\mathbf{v}]_{\text{std}} = P[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}$.
weaknesses.action: Before using $P$ or $P^{-1}$, write the sentence *"P eats B-coordinates"* in the margin. Redo problems 1 and 2 below.

weaknesses.title: Determinant row-operation rules under time pressure
weaknesses.misconception: Forgot that swapping two rows flips the sign of the determinant.
weaknesses.correction: Swapping rows is an odd permutation of the rows, so the sign flips. Scaling a row by $c$ multiplies the determinant by $c$; adding a multiple of one row to another changes nothing.

redo.what_went_wrong: Applied $P$ instead of $P^{-1}$: $P$ goes from $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates to standard, not the other way.
redo.hint: Which coordinates do you have, and which do you want? Write $\mathbf{v}$ as $a(1,1) + b(1,-1)$.
redo.solution: Solve $a + b = 3$, $a - b = 1$, so $a = 2$, $b = 1$ and $[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{B}} = (2, 1)$. Equivalently $[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{B}} = P^{-1}\mathbf{v}$ with $P = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}$ written as columns.

redo.problem: $T$ has matrix $A$ in the standard basis. Write the matrix of $T$ in basis $\mathcal{B}$ in terms of $A$ and $P$.
redo.what_went_wrong: Order reversed: you need to convert into standard coordinates first, apply $A$, then convert back.
redo.hint: Read the product right to left, as a pipeline acting on $[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}$.
redo.solution: $[T]_{\mathcal{B}} = P^{-1}AP$: $P$ turns $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates into standard ones, $A$ applies $T$, and $P^{-1}$ turns the result back into $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates.

redo.problem: Given $\det A = 5$ for a $3\times 3$ matrix $A$, find $\det B$ where $B$ is obtained by swapping rows 1 and 3 of $A$ and then multiplying row 2 by $4$.
redo.what_went_wrong: Missed the sign flip from the row swap.
